name: Altman's Z-score (original, public manufacturing firms)
prompt: Which weighted sum of five accounting ratios gives Altman's Z-score for a publicly traded manufacturing company?

variables.meaning: Altman Z-score; higher is more solvent (cut-off 2.675; above 3.0 unlikely to default, below 1.8 very high distress)
working capital / total assets
retained earnings / total assets
earnings before interest and taxes / total assets
market value of equity / book value of total liabilities (the only ratio not over total assets)
sales / total assets (asset turnover)

corruptions.why: The 3.3 weight belongs to EBIT/total assets (X_3), not to sales/total assets; X_5 carries roughly 1.
Working capital (X_1) takes 1.2 and retained earnings (X_2) takes 1.4, not the other way round.
Every weight is positive: more equity cushion relative to liabilities (X_4) raises the score.

sensitivities.why: More working capital per dollar of assets means more liquidity and a higher score.
More accumulated retained earnings signals cumulative profitability.
Higher operating return on assets carries the largest weight (3.3).
A bigger market equity cushion over liabilities makes insolvency less likely.
Higher asset turnover adds almost one-for-one to Z.

intuition: Liquidity, cumulative profit, operating profit, equity cushion and turnover: the recipe weights are 1.2, 1.4, 3.3, 0.6, ~1, and EBIT earns the biggest weight.

name: Marginal (unconditional) PD from a cumulative default table
prompt: From a table of cumulative default rates, how do you get the unconditional probability of defaulting during year t?

variables.meaning: probability, viewed from today, of defaulting during year t
probability of defaulting by the end of year t (read directly from the table)
probability of defaulting by the end of year t-1
year (time horizon) of interest

corruptions.why: Cumulative PD only rises with t, so this order gives a negative probability.
Dividing by survival gives the conditional PD, not the unconditional (marginal) one.
The table is cumulative; the year-t figure must have the previous year's cumulative stripped out.

sensitivities.why: More cumulative default by year-end, holding the prior year fixed, means more default inside year t.
More of the cumulative total already happened before year t, leaving less for year t itself.

intuition: Everything in the table is cumulative; the marginal PD is just the step up from one column to the next.

name: Conditional PD in year t given survival
prompt: What is the probability of defaulting in year t given no default before year t, from the marginal PD and the survival probability?

variables.meaning: probability of defaulting in year t given survival to the start of year t
unconditional probability of defaulting during year t = Cumulative PD(t) - Cumulative PD(t-1)
probability of no default by end of year t-1 = 1 - Cumulative PD(t-1)
year of interest

corruptions.why: Upside down: this gives a number far above 1, not a probability.
You condition on having survived, so divide by 1 - Cumulative PD(t-1), not by the cumulative PD itself.
Survival is measured to the START of year t, i.e. to t-1, not to the end of year t.

sensitivities.why: More unconditional default in year t means more default among survivors too.
The same marginal PD spread over a larger surviving population is a smaller conditional chance.

intuition: Conditional PD rescales the marginal PD to the survivors only, so it is always at least as large as the marginal PD.

name: Cumulative probability of default by time t from the hazard rate
prompt: Given the average hazard rate (default intensity) from 0 to t, what is the cumulative probability of default by time t?

variables.meaning: cumulative probability of default by time t
average hazard rate (default intensity) between time 0 and t, per year, decimal
time horizon in years

corruptions.why: That is the survival probability to t; the default probability is one minus it.
Without the minus in the exponent the result is negative; survival must decay with time.
The hazard rate is per year, so it is multiplied by the horizon, not divided by it.

sensitivities.why: A higher default intensity makes survival decay faster.
Cumulative default can only grow with a longer horizon.

intuition: Survival decays exponentially at the hazard rate; default is whatever has not survived.

name: Average hazard rate from a credit spread
prompt: How do you back out the average hazard rate from a credit (CDS or bond yield) spread and the recovery rate?

variables.meaning: average hazard rate up to maturity T, per year, decimal
credit spread for maturity T (a CDS spread or bond yield spread), decimal (210 bp = 0.021)
recovery rate, decimal; 1 - RR is the loss given default

corruptions.why: The spread compensates for what is LOST on default, so gross it up by 1 - RR, not by RR.
Spread is roughly hazard rate times LGD, so the hazard rate is spread divided by LGD, not multiplied.

sensitivities.why: A wider spread signals more default risk.
With higher recovery each default costs less, so the same spread must imply more frequent default.

intuition: Spread is roughly default frequency times loss per default, so divide the spread by the loss given default.

name: Forward hazard rate between year 3 and year 5 (time-weighted blend)
prompt: How does the 5-year average hazard rate relate to the 3-year average and the forward hazard rate for years 3 to 5?

variables.meaning: average hazard rate from 0 to year 5, decimal
average hazard rate from 0 to year 3, decimal
average (forward) hazard rate between year 3 and year 5, decimal

corruptions.why: Average rates must be weighted by the years they cover before they can be added.
The forward rate covers only the two years from 3 to 5, so its weight is 2.
The five-year total is the first three years PLUS the next two.

sensitivities.why: A higher hazard over the first three years raises the cumulative five-year total.
A higher hazard in years 3 to 5 raises the cumulative five-year total.

intuition: Hazard-rate-years add up: five years at the 5-year average equals three years at the 3-year average plus two years at the forward rate.

name: CDS-bond basis
prompt: How is the CDS-bond basis defined from the two measures of the same credit risk?

variables.meaning: gap between the two credit spreads; should be zero or near zero
annual cost of CDS protection on the reference entity, in bp of notional
yield on the corporate bond minus yield on a comparable risk-free bond

corruptions.why: The basis is CDS minus bond; flipping it reverses every positive/negative-basis conclusion.
Spread minus fixed coupon drives the up-front premium, not the basis.

sensitivities.why: Dearer protection pushes the basis positive.
A wider bond spread pushes the basis negative.

intuition: Two prices for the same default risk; the basis is CDS minus bond, and anything that gives the protection buyer an extra option pushes it positive.

name: Merton model: value of equity today
prompt: In the Merton model, what is today's value of the firm's equity as a call on the firm's assets?

variables.meaning: market value of the firm's equity today
value of the firm's assets today (not directly observable)
face value of the debt due at T (the strike)
risk-free rate, continuously compounded, decimal
time to debt maturity in years
cumulative standard normal distribution function
(ln(V_0/D) + (r + sigma_V^2/2)T) / (sigma_V sqrt(T))
d_1 - sigma_V sqrt(T)

corruptions.why: N(d_1) is the delta that multiplies the asset value; N(d_2) goes with the discounted debt.
The debt is paid at T, so it must be discounted by e^{-rT}.
Equity is a call: shareholders get assets MINUS the debt they must repay.

sensitivities.why: Higher asset value makes the call on the assets more valuable.
A higher strike (more debt to repay) lowers the call value.
A higher rate lowers the present value of the debt the shareholders owe.
Equity is a call on the assets, and a call gains value when the underlying is more volatile (limited downside, unlimited upside).

intuition: Equity is a Black-Scholes call on the firm's assets struck at the face value of the debt.

name: Merton model: d1
prompt: In the Merton equity formula, how is d1 computed from asset value, debt, the risk-free rate, asset volatility and maturity?

variables.meaning: first Black-Scholes-Merton argument; N(d_1) is the equity's delta with respect to assets
value of the firm's assets today
face value of debt due at T
risk-free rate, decimal
volatility of the firm's asset value, decimal per year
time to debt maturity in years

corruptions.why: With minus half the variance this is d_2, not d_1.
The log-moneyness is assets over debt; a firm with assets well above debt must have a large positive d_1.
Volatility scales with the square root of time, so the denominator is sigma_V times sqrt(T).

sensitivities.why: More assets relative to debt pushes the option deeper in the money.
More debt raises the strike.
Assets drift up faster under the risk-neutral measure.

intuition: Standardised log-distance of assets above the debt, with the drift at r plus half the variance.

name: Merton model: d2 from d1
prompt: In the Merton model, how is d2 obtained from d1?

variables.meaning: second BSM argument; the distance to default; N(-d_2) is the risk-neutral PD
first BSM argument
volatility of the firm's asset value, decimal
time to debt maturity in years

corruptions.why: d_2 is always the smaller of the two: subtract one standard deviation over the horizon.
The horizon enters through sqrt(T), not T.

sensitivities.why: d_2 moves one-for-one with d_1.
Holding d_1 fixed, a larger volatility gap is subtracted.
Holding d_1 fixed, a longer horizon subtracts more.

intuition: d_2 sits exactly one horizon-standard-deviation below d_1.

name: Merton model: equity volatility vs asset volatility (Ito's lemma)
prompt: What second equation (from Ito's lemma) links observable equity volatility to the unobservable asset volatility in the Merton model?
latex: \sigma_E E_0 = \frac{\partial E}{\partial V}\sigma_V V_0 = N(d_1)\sigma_V V_0

variables.meaning: volatility of the firm's equity (observable/estimable), decimal
market value of equity today (observable)
delta of equity with respect to asset value, equal to N(d_1)
cumulative standard normal at d_1
volatility of the firm's asset value (unobservable), decimal
value of the firm's assets today (unobservable)

corruptions.why: The equity's delta with respect to assets is N(d_1), not N(d_2).
Each volatility is paired with its own value: sigma_E with E_0 and sigma_V with V_0.
Dropping the values ignores leverage; equity volatility is much larger than asset volatility because E_0 is small relative to V_0.

sensitivities.why: A larger equity delta passes more of the asset volatility through to equity.
More volatile assets make a more volatile equity claim.
A bigger asset base behind each dollar of equity means more dollar volatility.

intuition: Dollar volatility of equity = delta times dollar volatility of assets; leverage is why sigma_E far exceeds sigma_V.

name: Merton distance to default (d2)
prompt: How many standard deviations are the firm's assets from the default point? Give the Merton distance to default.

variables.meaning: distance to default: standard deviations between asset value and the face value of debt
second BSM argument, equal to DtD
value of the firm's assets today
face value of debt (the default point)
risk-free rate, decimal (replace by expected asset return mu for the real-world version)
volatility of asset value, decimal
time horizon (debt maturity) in years

corruptions.why: Plus half the variance gives d_1; the distance to default is d_2, with minus.
Distance is measured from the debt UP to the assets: ln V_0 minus ln D.
The standard deviation over the horizon is sigma_V times sqrt(T).

sensitivities.why: More assets relative to debt puts the firm further from default.
More debt moves the default point closer.
Faster expected asset growth moves assets away from the default point.
Falls with volatility whenever ln(V_0/D) + rT is positive (assets comfortably above the debt, the normal case); a deeply distressed firm can see it rise.

intuition: The log-cushion of assets over debt, grown at the drift, measured in horizon standard deviations: the bigger it is, the smaller the PD.

name: Merton risk-neutral probability of default
prompt: In the Merton model, what is the risk-neutral probability that the firm defaults (shareholders do not exercise)?

variables.meaning: risk-neutral probability of default by T (assets end below the debt)
cumulative standard normal distribution function
distance to default

corruptions.why: N(d_2) is the risk-neutral probability the option IS exercised, i.e. of survival.
The exercise probability uses d_2; d_1 belongs to the delta.

sensitivities.why: A greater distance to default means a lower probability of default.

intuition: Default = the call finishes out of the money, which has probability N(-d_2).

name: Replicating portfolio: up-state condition
prompt: In the six-month call on a zero example, what condition must the replicating portfolio of six-month and one-year zeros meet in the up state (rate 2.50%)?

variables.meaning: face value of six-month zeros bought on date 0 (negative = short); pays its face in the up state
face value of one-year zeros bought on date 0; worth 0.987654 per dollar of face in the up state

corruptions.why: 0.992556 is the six-month zero price in the DOWN state (rate 1.50%); the up state uses 0.987654.
The call is worthless in the up state; $2.556 is the down-state payoff.
Those are date-0 prices, used to price the portfolio, not its value on date 1.

sensitivities.why: Each extra dollar of six-month face adds a dollar in the up state.
Each dollar of one-year face is worth 0.987654 in the up state.

intuition: Match the option state by state: in the up state the call is worthless, so the portfolio must be worth zero there.

name: Replicating portfolio: down-state condition
prompt: In the six-month call on a zero example, what condition must the replicating portfolio meet in the down state (rate 1.50%)?

variables.meaning: face value of six-month zeros bought on date 0 (negative = short); pays its face on date 1
face value of one-year zeros bought on date 0; worth 0.992556 per dollar of face in the down state

corruptions.why: 0.987654 is the up-state price (rate 2.50%); in the down state the zero is worth 0.992556.
In the down state the call pays 992.556 - 990 = $2.556, not zero.

sensitivities.why: Each extra dollar of six-month face adds a dollar in the down state.
Each dollar of one-year face is worth 0.992556 in the down state.

intuition: In the down state the zero is worth $992.556, so the call pays $2.556 and the portfolio must too.

name: Option price = date-0 cost of the replicating portfolio
prompt: Once F^5 and F^1 are solved, how is the call priced by the law of one price from today's zero prices?

variables.meaning: date-0 price of the call on the zero ($0.504 in the example)
face of six-month zeros in the replicating portfolio (-$515.00: a short); today's price 0.990099 per dollar
face of one-year zeros in the replicating portfolio ($521.4375); today's price 0.978842 per dollar

corruptions.why: The six-month zero is the dearer one today (0.990099); the one-year zero is 0.978842.
Those are date-1 state prices; the replicating portfolio is costed at today's prices.

sensitivities.why: More six-month face costs more today.
More one-year face costs more today.

intuition: Same payoffs in every state means same price today: the option costs exactly what its replicating bonds cost.

name: CMT swap payoff at a node ($1,000,000 notional, semiannual)
prompt: What is the semiannual payoff of a $1,000,000-notional constant-maturity Treasury swap at a node, from the CMT yield and the fixed rate?

variables.meaning: swap payoff at that node, floating (CMT) minus fixed, $ (positive when the CMT yield is above the fixed rate)
semiannually compounded yield of a predetermined maturity observed on the payment date (the node's rate), decimal
the swap's fixed rate, decimal (7.00% in the worked example)

corruptions.why: The payoff is floating (CMT) minus fixed: a 7.25% node against a 7.00% fixed rate pays +$1,250.
Payments are semiannual, so the annual rate difference accrues on half the notional.

sensitivities.why: A higher CMT yield at the node raises what the CMT receiver is paid.
A higher fixed rate raises what the CMT receiver pays away.

intuition: Half a year's worth of the rate gap on the notional: (notional / 2) times (CMT minus fixed).
